guide.title: Derivatives in Calculus
guide.text:
## Derivatives in Calculus

A **derivative** measures how fast a function changes. It tells the **slope of the tangent line** to a curve at a point, so it is useful for motion, growth, and optimization.

### 1) Basic Idea

For a function \(f(x)\), the derivative is written as:

\[
f'(x) \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{dy}{dx}
\]

The formal definition is:

\[
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
\]

This means we look at the average rate of change over a tiny interval, then let that interval shrink to 0.

If \(f'(x) > 0\), the function is increasing.  
If \(f'(x) < 0\), the function is decreasing.  
If \(f'(x) = 0\), the graph may have a flat point or a turning point.

### 2) Common Rules

- **Power rule:** \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}\)
- **Constant rule:** \(\frac{d}{dx}(c)=0\)
- **Constant multiple rule:** \(\frac{d}{dx}[cf(x)] = c f'(x)\)
- **Sum rule:** \(\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)+g(x)] = f'(x)+g'(x)\)

These rules make derivatives much faster to compute than using the limit every time.

### 3) Worked Example

Find the derivative of \(f(x)=x^2+3x\).

\[
\frac{d}{dx}(x^2+3x) = \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) + \frac{d}{dx}(3x)
\]

\[
= 2x + 3
\]

So,

\[
f'(x)=2x+3
\]

At \(x=2\), the slope is \(f'(2)=7\).

### 4) Why It Matters

Derivatives help estimate change. For example, if a quantity is growing by 5%, the derivative describes that rate at an instant. In physics, if position is \(s(t)\), then velocity is \(s'(t)\).

Useful constants: \(e \approx 2.71828\), \(\pi \approx 3.14159\).

script.title: Derivatives in Calculus: Slope, Rate, and Rules
script.description: A short StudyMesh-style recap of what derivatives mean, how they’re defined, and the key rules and example from the study guide.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Welcome back! Today we’re studying derivatives in calculus—what they mean and how to compute them.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Right. The core idea is that a derivative measures how fast a function changes. Geometrically, it gives the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a point.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: And that’s why derivatives show up in motion, growth, and optimization. If you know the slope at an instant, you can estimate change more precisely.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Let’s pin down the notation. For a function f(x), the derivative is written as f'(x) or dy/dx.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: The formal definition uses a limit: f'(x) = lim_{h→0} (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h. We start with an average rate of change over a tiny interval, then shrink the interval to zero.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: So the sign of the derivative tells you about the graph. If f'(x) > 0, the function is increasing. If f'(x) < 0, it’s decreasing. And if f'(x) = 0, the graph may have a flat point or a turning point.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Now, computing derivatives directly from the limit every time would be slow. That’s why we use common rules.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: First is the power rule: d/dx (x^n) = n x^{n−1}. Then the constant rule: d/dx (c) = 0.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: We also have the constant multiple rule: d/dx [c f(x)] = c f'(x). And the sum rule: d/dx [f(x) + g(x)] = f'(x) + g'(x). These rules make derivatives much faster to compute.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Let’s do the worked example from the guide. Find the derivative of f(x) = x^2 + 3x.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: We differentiate term by term: d/dx (x^2 + 3x) = d/dx (x^2) + d/dx (3x). Using the power rule and the constant multiple rule, that becomes 2x + 3.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: So f'(x) = 2x + 3. And at x = 2, the slope is f'(2) = 7.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Great. Now, why does this matter beyond the algebra? Derivatives help estimate change—like describing a growth rate at an instant.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: The guide also connects it to physics: if position is s(t), then velocity is s'(t). So the derivative translates “how position changes” into “how fast it’s moving.”

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: And as a quick note, the study guide lists useful constants: e ≈ 2.71828 and π ≈ 3.14159.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: That’s the big picture: derivatives measure instantaneous change, equal the tangent slope, and can be computed efficiently using the power, constant, constant multiple, and sum rules.

script.title: Derivatives in Calculus: How Fast Things Change
script.description: A short, warm conversation about what derivatives mean, how to interpret their sign, the main derivative rules, and a worked example for f of x equals x squared plus three x.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Welcome back. Today we are talking about derivatives in calculus, and the big idea is simple: a derivative measures how fast a function changes.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Right. And it is not just speed in the everyday sense. A derivative tells the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a point, which is why it shows up in motion, growth, and optimization.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Let’s anchor it. For a function f of x, the derivative is written as f prime of x, or as dy over dx. Formally, it is the limit as h goes to zero of f of x plus h minus f of x, all over h.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: So we start with an average rate of change over a tiny interval, then shrink the interval until it becomes zero. That is how we get the instantaneous rate.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Now the sign matters. If f prime of x is greater than zero, the function is increasing. If f prime of x is less than zero, it is decreasing. And if f prime of x equals zero, the graph may have a flat point or a turning point.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Quick question for you. When you hear f prime of x equals zero, do you think it always means a turning point?

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Good catch. Not always. The idea is that the graph may have a flat point or a turning point, so zero derivative signals something special, but we still look at the shape.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Exactly. Now, computing derivatives by that limit every time would be painful, so we use common rules. The power rule says the derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus one.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: And the constant rule says the derivative of a constant c is zero. There is also the constant multiple rule: the derivative of c times f of x is c times f prime of x. Plus the sum rule: the derivative of f of x plus g of x is f prime of x plus g prime of x.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Let’s do the worked example. We want the derivative of f of x equals x squared plus three x. Using the sum rule, the derivative of x squared plus the derivative of three x.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Then apply the power rule to x squared, which gives two x. And for three x, treat it as three times x, so the derivative is three times the derivative of x, which is just three. Put together, f prime of x equals two x plus three.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: And at x equals two, the slope is f prime of two equals seven. That is the tangent line slope at that point, not an average over an interval.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Why does this matter beyond slopes? Derivatives help estimate change. For example, if a quantity is growing by five percent, the derivative describes that rate at an instant.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: In physics language, if position is s of t, then velocity is s prime of t. So the derivative connects how something moves to how its position changes over time.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: One more thing I like to remember is that calculus also uses important constants. We have e, roughly two point seven, and pi, roughly three point one four. They show up in deeper derivative and growth ideas, even though today we focused on the core definition and rules.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: So to recap in plain terms: a derivative is the instantaneous rate of change, it matches the tangent line slope, and the sign tells whether the function rises or falls. Then the power, constant, constant multiple, and sum rules let us compute quickly.
